title: Greater than our heart (1 John 3:19–24)
hook: when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: in deed and in truth, and the gut feeling love doesn't shut off. Your line was not in word only.

Some people have a prosecutor living in their head. It replays the awkward thing you said at the party. It reminds you of the mistake from ten years ago. It says, you call that love? After a passage about loving in deed and in truth, that voice can get loud: did I do enough? Have I ever really loved anyone that way? The writer of First John seems to know his own words can set it off. So right after asking for real, costly love, he turns to the reader whose heart is condemning them.

He says that by loving in deed we know we are of the truth, and "shall assure our hearts before him." Assure, here, means to calm, to persuade, to quiet down. Then the line: "For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things." Christians have heard this in two ways, and it's honest to say so. One reading hears comfort: your heart is a harsh judge, but not the final one. God is greater; he knows everything, including what you've forgotten, the good you did and the reasons you struggled, and, on this reading, he is merciful. Some older commentators heard a warning instead: if even your own heart condemns you, how much more does God, who knows all things? Both readings take God's knowledge seriously. Readers who favor comfort point to the paragraph's purpose, which is to settle the heart. Then: "Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God." Confidence is a word for freedom of speech, speaking openly, like a child who isn't afraid to ask. And he sums up the whole commandment in one sentence: "That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another." Believe and love: two halves of one command. Last, he names how we know God lives in us: by the Spirit he has given us. In this letter, the heart is a witness, not the final judge.
screen: then, large: `GOD IS GREATER THAN OUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Let the inner prosecutor speak for a moment, and hear it out without arguing. Then imagine something bigger standing beside that voice, not to shout it down but to know more than it knows: the context it forgot, the good it skipped, the reasons it ignored. Breathe out, let your shoulders drop, and if you pray, bring the accusation to God and leave it there.
Confidence. First John's word for freedom of speech, speaking openly before God like a child unafraid to ask, when the heart does not condemn.
Your line: greater than your heart. Believe and love, one command in two halves. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Pastors and spiritual directors sometimes turn to 1 John 3:20 with people troubled by guilt or a harsh conscience, and some Christians memorize it as a comfort.

notes: Two readings of 3:20 (comfort vs. warning): the warning reading is associated with some older commentators (e.g. some Reformation-era readings); the comfort reading is widely held today. Confirm characterization.
'For the first time in the letter, he names ... the Spirit' (3:24): the Spirit is not mentioned in 1 John before 3:24 (the 'anointing' of 2:20, 27 is related). Please confirm.
πείσομεν (3:19), KJV 'assure', glossed as persuade/calm. Confirm.
παρρησία (3:21) as freedom of speech/boldness. Confirm.
